newsitem.title: CANADA: Autopsies show Canada cult victims died in fire.
newsitem.headline: Autopsies show Canada cult victims died in fire.

text.p: Four of the five Solar Temple cult members involved in a group suicide last week died of smoke inhalation, a Quebec coroner reported on Thursday.
Firefighters discovered the five victims on Saturday in a burned-out house in the village of Saint Casimir 37 miles (60 km) outside of Quebec City.
Quebec coroner Dr. Yvon Naud told a news conference two men and two women found lying in the form of a cross on a bed on the second floor of the house died from carbon monoxide poisoning.
"In these four people, the respiratory tracts were heavily soiled by soot, which signifies that they were alive at the time of the fire," Naud said.

Another woman found on a ground-floor sofa with a nylon cloth covering her head was dead when the blaze began, Naud said. He said there were no signs she had been murdered but she may have died from swallowing substances or drugs.

Two of the victims found upstairs were Didier Queze, 39, and his wife Chantal Goupillot-Queze, 41, both French citizens. The 63-year-old woman found downstairs on the sofa was Suzanne Druau, Goupillot's mother and the grandmother of three teenagers who survived the group suicide.

All five bodies had quantities of a mixture of over-the-counter sedatives, hypnotics, anti-convulsives and muscle relaxants, Naud said. All five bodies had burns, but none had bullet wounds or other signs of violence.

The teenagers emerged from a nearby shed as firefighters fought the blaze and later told police their parents included them without their knowledge in the group's first suicide attempt on March 20, coinciding with the spring equinox.

But a crude incendiary device fashioned of propane tanks, electric elements and fuel containers did not work then because of a faulty timer. The parents then granted the children's request that they be excluded from the second suicide attempt two days later.
A spokesman for the Quebec youth protection agency, which has taken custody of them, said they were "doing well" and were being counselled by social workers and psychologists.

Quebec provincial police Lt. Alain Quirion said police were examining the actions of the five victims and three children between the first and second suicide attempts, and would file a report with the prosecutor's office on Wednesday.
"The report will be given to the Crown prosecutor so that he can decide the responsibilities and actions of each one," Quirion said.
Quirion said Canada's Young Offenders Act prevented him from divulging what the children told police about their possible involvement in starting the fatal fire.
The Solar Temple is an international doomsday cult whose members believe a ritualized death takes them on a journey to a new life on the star Sirius.

Since 1994, 74 cult members and others have been killed in group suicides and murders in Quebec, France and Switzerland. Some of the victims, including children and an infant, were shot, poisoned, stabbed or asphyxiated with plastic bags.

A one-page letter stamped March 21 by a post office near Saint Casimir and sent to four Quebec French-language newspapers by the fire victims indicates they had been planning their group suicide since the first cult deaths in Quebec and Switzerland in October 1994.

Those events, a second group of murder-suicides in France in December 1995 and the Saint Casimir deaths are "departures" for Sirius that are part of the same process, it said. "These three departures are in effect one and the same transit."
The letter, a copy of which police found at the Saint Casimir property, appears to have been sent by Queze to the media and the victims' families.

It contains a veiled threat against Thierry Huguenin, a former member of the sect now living in Switzerland who wrote a book entitled "Le 54e," (The 54th), a reference to his escaping the first group of murder-suicides in which 48 people died in Switzerland and five died in Quebec.
"As for the pseudo 54th, he should know that the welcoming committee awaits him," the letter said.

In the United States, 39 members of another cult were found dead on Wednesday in a million-dollar mansion in Rancho Sante Fe, an exclusive community near San Diego. Investigators said the group apparently committed suicide in the belief a UFO, shielded behind a comet, would take them to heaven.
Quebec provincial police special investigator Nadine Tremblay said the force would contact California officials to obtain more information about the San Diego suicides.
